name: Millionaire
seoDesc: Millionaire: work out your result from the I would like to save.. and the initial savings. A free finance calculator with the formula, units and a worked…
summary:
Supply the I would like to save.., the initial savings, the annual interest rate and the additional deposits and the Millionaire calculator solves for the answer. It suits a budget, a loan conversation, a payslip check or a what-if before you talk to a lender.

The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Millionaire calculator work?
sections.html:
The Millionaire calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationships described below and reports every result it can derive from them.

Working from the top of the form: you choose the option that describes your case (the compound frequency); then you type in the I would like to save.., the initial savings, the annual interest rate and the additional deposits.

Press Calculate and the page works through the equation with the values you supplied and derives the rest; it then keeps up with you as you correct a typo.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Millionaire calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Additional deposits made at the=(-100 × compound frequency × additional deposits × (1 + (1 ÷ 100) × annual interest rate ÷ compound frequency, compound frequency × duration to reach goal) + 100 × compound frequency × additional deposits − initial savings × annual interest rate × (1 + (1 ÷ 100) × annual interest rate ÷ compound frequency, compound frequency × duration to reach goal) + annual interest rate × I would like to save..) ÷ (annual interest rate × additional deposits × ((1 + (1 ÷ 100) × annual interest rate ÷ compound frequency, compound frequency × duration to reach goal) − 1))
Future worth of $1 million in today's dollars=(10 ^ 6 − 2 × duration to reach goal) × (100 − inflation rate ^ duration to reach goal)

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
The form opens with a complete set of values: I would like to save.. = 1000000, Initial savings = 20000, Annual interest rate = 4 and Compound frequency set to Monthly. Straight away the calculator returns Duration to reach goal = 0.0098 hrs and Future worth of $1 million in today's dollars = 492046.

Those are real numbers produced by the same engine that runs when you press Calculate, so you can change any single box afterwards and watch the answer move from this starting point.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Duration to reach goal = 0.0098 hrs and Future worth of $1 million in today's dollars = 492046 should be roughly the size you expected from I would like to save.. = 1000000 and Initial savings = 20000.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
• The option the calculation settles on.
  • Shown in US Dollar, and convertible to any of the 113 units on that chip.

If a number looks wrong, check three things in this order: that the units match what you had in mind, that no drop-down is still on its default, and that the value you entered is on the same scale as the rest — a rate typed as 5 rather than 0.05 is the classic mistake. Those three account for almost every answer that is out by a factor.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar
  • Time, opening in years / months
  • Currency, opening in US Dollar

Display rounding is separate from calculation rounding: the digits you see are shortened, the value behind them is not. Numbers far from everyday size are shown in scientific notation so the significant digits stay readable.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Millionaire calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Sizing up a purchase before you commit to it
  • Comparing two offers that quote their costs in different ways
  • Building a monthly budget and testing how one number shifts the rest
  • Any time the same 4 figures keep coming back — the I would like to save.., the initial savings and the annual interest rate — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • If a result surprises you, look at the order of magnitude before the digits: a plausible number in the wrong unit looks more convincing than an implausible one, and is easier to miss.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html:
• Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.
  • Answers that depend on a drop-down reflect the option you picked, not a range. Switching to a neighbouring option is the quickest way to see how much that factor matters.
  • Some options are backed by reference tables that ship with the page, so the values are fixed data rather than a live lookup.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Millionaire calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the I would like to save.., the initial savings, the annual interest rate and the additional deposits, which is 7 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter I would like to save.. in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. I would like to save.. opens in US Dollar and the chip beside it offers 113 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

faq.q: How much do the drop-down choices change the answer?
faq.a: There are several choices to make (2 in total), and each one selects a different case rather than scaling the result. Switching a single option and watching the result is the fastest way to see how much that choice is worth.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Duration to reach goal = 0.0098 hrs. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Millionaire calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
